burning = Simulation(forest, dt=1).check().prepare().run(until=3).trajectory_.lattice('forest.fire')
print([int(item.sum()) for item in burning])

Lattices on graphs. LatticeElement also takes a NetworkSpace, with one site per node in the order of graph.nodes, and initial values as arrays in node order or mappings from node to value. AdjacencyNeighborhood(center=False) is the neighbourhood of a node, its neighbours along its edges, padded to the largest degree with the network's fill value. Local rules, drives, relaxations, Monte Carlo laws, and extremal laws run on graphs as on lattices. Lookup rules on graphs take the totalistic forms, and a function rule that names the keyword degree receives the number of real neighbours of every site. The padded table grows with the largest degree, so graphs with hubs of very high degree, beyond scale-free graphs of about 10^5 nodes, use much memory.

Neighbour sums and colored schedules. neighbors(expression, reduce='sum') sums an expression of a site and one neighbour, read through s.other, over the real neighbours of the site, so local energies are exact on sites of any degree and outside fixed edges. schedule='colored' on local rules and samplers updates the classes of a proper coloring of the neighbour graph in turn, which NetworkX computes once per law. The checkerboard schedule stays the two-color case of square lattices.

from typing import Annotated

import networkx as nx
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import ZZ

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import SampleLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import neighbors
from skcomplex.core.spaces import AdjacencyNeighborhood, NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.specs import MoveSpec, ObjectiveSpec, ParameterSpec, SamplerSpec, StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


class GraphSpinElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        spin: Annotated[float, StateSpec(domain=ZZ)] = 1.0,
        J: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
        temperature: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.spin = spin
        self.J = J
        self.temperature = temperature

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        energy = -s.J * s.spin * neighbors(s.other.spin, reduce='sum')
        sampler = SamplerSpec('metropolis', 1 / s.temperature, schedule='colored')
        return [SampleLaw(ObjectiveSpec(energy, AdjacencyNeighborhood()), MoveSpec(s.spin, 'flip'), sampler)]


graph = nx.random_regular_graph(4, 200, seed=0)
spins = System(elements=[LatticeElement('spins', element=GraphSpinElement, space=NetworkSpace(graph))])
print(abs(Simulation(spins, dt=50, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=200).state_.mean()) > 0.9)

Extremal updates. ExtremalLaw(targets, over, rule, key=None, extremum='min', repeat=1) finds the site with the smallest or largest value of a key state, breaking ties with the simulation's random stream, and applies rule(*values, random, **parameters) to the site and its real neighbours, repeat times per step. Every application is recorded among the trajectory's events as an ExtremalRecord with its time, site, and extremal value. On the Numba backend the applications of a step run in one compiled loop when Numba compiles the rule, which then takes its arguments by position or keyword, with no keyword-only arguments, and both backends give the same events.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import ExtremalLaw
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeNeighborhood, LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


def renew(fitness, random):
    return random


class SpeciesElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, fitness: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.5):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.fitness = fitness

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [ExtremalLaw(s.fitness, LatticeNeighborhood(((-1,), (1,))), renew, repeat=100, label='extinction')]


fitness = np.random.default_rng(0).random(100)
space = LatticeSpace(100)
ring = System(elements=[LatticeElement('ring', element=SpeciesElement, space=space, values={'fitness': fitness})])
trajectory = Simulation(ring, dt=10, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=100).trajectory_
print(len(trajectory.events), trajectory.events[0].label)

Square lattice groups stream to Rerun as images colored by value, and triangular lattices and graph lattices stream as sites with SiteVisual: hexagonal cells at the site positions, or nodes colored by state with their edges logged once. The library has elementary_automaton, game_of_life, majority_rule, langtons_ant, nagel_schreckenberg, hodgepodge, sandpile, forest_fire, hexagonal_forest_fire, earthquakes, ising, graph_ising, potts, xy, fhp_lattice_gas, and bak_sneppen, each in the subfield of its science, such as skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata for game_of_life and skcomplex.models.physics.statistical_mechanics for ising.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: A NetworkSpace holds a NetworkX graph whose nodes carry the members of groups on its sites and whose edges carry the members of groups on its edges. The states and the structure of a network can change together: interactions read and change edge states, laws reduce over the neighbours of a node, and topology requests add and remove nodes and edges.

docs.title: Generators and layers
docs.text:
A NetworkSpace takes any NetworkX graph, so the generators of NetworkX build it, such as nx.erdos_renyi_graph, nx.watts_strogatz_graph, or nx.barabasi_albert_graph. A generator takes a seed, so a network drawn for an experiment is reproducible, and node positions in the node attribute pos, as nx.random_geometric_graph sets them, become the fitted positions_. A LayerSpec names a second relation over the same nodes, such as work next to contacts. Preparing a network lowers every layer to arrays by its label, None for the graph itself: graphs_ holds its graph, edges_ the source and target of every edge, and adjacency_ the neighbours of every node in compressed sparse row form.

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.specs import LayerSpec

first = NetworkSpace(nx.watts_strogatz_graph(100, 6, 0.1, seed=7))
second = NetworkSpace(nx.watts_strogatz_graph(100, 6, 0.1, seed=7))
print(sorted(first.graph.edges) == sorted(second.graph.edges))

space = NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(4), layers=[LayerSpec('work', nx.complete_graph(4))]).check().prepare()
print(list(space.graphs_), [item.tolist() for item in space.edges_['work']])

docs.title: Interactions over edges
docs.text:
A group on the edges of a network, GroupElement(..., on='edges'), holds one member per edge of its layer. A NeighborInteraction binds a group on the nodes and, optionally, a group on the edges of the same network. Its laws run once per edge and read s.source, s.target, and s.edge: the members at both ends and the member of the edge. Rate, noise, and jump laws may target any of them, and update laws the edge member. The argument layer chooses the layer of an interaction without an edge group. Hebbian weights grow with the product of the activities at the ends:

from typing import Annotated

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import NeighborInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, RoleSpec, StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


class NeuronElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, a: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.a = a


class SynapseElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, w: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.1):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.w = w


class HebbianInteraction(NeighborInteraction):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        neurons: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        synapses: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        eta: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.neurons = neurons
        self.synapses = synapses
        self.eta = eta

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.edge.w, s.eta * s.source.a * s.target.a)]


space = NetworkSpace(nx.cycle_graph(6))
system = System(
    elements=[
        LatticeElement('neurons', element=NeuronElement, space=space, values={'a': [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]}),
        GroupElement('synapses', element=SynapseElement, space=space, on='edges'),
    ],
    interactions=[HebbianInteraction('hebb', neurons='neurons', synapses='synapses')],
)
trajectory = Simulation(system, dt=0.5).check().prepare().run(until=1.0).trajectory_
print(np.round(trajectory.values('synapses.w')[-1], 3).tolist())

docs.title: Hypergraphs and laws per hyperedge
docs.text:
A network space holds hyperedges beside its edges: NetworkSpace(graph, hyperedges=...) takes sequences of at least two nodes, an XGI Hypergraph, or an XGI SimplicialComplex, whose faces of at least two nodes are its hyperedges. The members of an XGI hyperedge follow the order of the nodes of the graph. The prepared space holds hyperedges_, the node indices of every hyperedge, incidence_, the sparse incidence matrix of nodes and hyperedges, and memberships_, the hyperedges around every node.

A HyperedgeInteraction binds a group on the nodes and runs its laws once per hyperedge, on the hyperedges of its size or of every size when the size is None. The laws read s.member, the focal member, s.others, the other members in hyperedge order, and s.members, which total, mean, count, maximum, and minimum reduce with over=s.members. A law of the focal member runs once per member of every hyperedge and adds into that member. The compiler builds one gather table per size of hyperedge, so the laws run as gathers and scatter-adds on the NumPy and Numba backends. A second role may bind a group on the hyperedges, read as s.hyperedge, or a group on the edges, read as s.edge, the edge that joins the first two members of the hyperedge. A law that targets either runs once per hyperedge. Three-body phase coupling over the triangles of a hypergraph:

from typing import Annotated

import itertools
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import xgi
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import sin

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import HyperedgeInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.compile import compile_system
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, RoleSpec, StateSpec


class PhaseElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, theta: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.theta = theta


class TriadInteraction(HyperedgeInteraction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, phases: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], K: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label, size=3)
        self.phases = phases
        self.K = K

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        first, second = (other.theta for other in s.others)
        return [RateLaw(s.member.theta, s.K * sin(first + second - 2 * s.member.theta))]


triangles = xgi.Hypergraph([list(nodes) for nodes in itertools.combinations(range(5), 3)])
space = NetworkSpace(nx.complete_graph(5), hyperedges=triangles)
system = System(
    elements=[LatticeElement('phases', element=PhaseElement, space=space, values={'theta': np.linspace(0, 1, 5)})],
    interactions=[TriadInteraction('triads', phases='phases')],
)
problem = compile_system(system)
drift = problem.drift(0.0, problem.initial_state, problem.initial_parameters)
print(len(space.check().prepare().hyperedges_), np.round(drift, 3).tolist())

The compiler reports an interaction whose size no hyperedge of the network has, and an edge group whose edge does not join the first two members of a hyperedge, with the issue code binding.

docs.title: Symbolic groupings
docs.text:
GroupingInteraction(form='symbolic', write=..., function=..., reduce='sum') runs a function of one group on the same path as the laws per hyperedge: the groups of a step are its hyperedges. The function reads the namespace of one group, s.member, the member it gives a value to, s.others, and s.members, and returns the value of the state write for that member in the next step, so the system runs in discrete time. A member takes the sum, or with reduce='mean' the mean, of the values of the groups that hold it, and a member in no group keeps its value.

  • 'pairs' and 'partition' are drawn again at every step from the random stream of the simulation, so two runs with one seed draw the same groups, on the NumPy and the Numba backends alike.
  • 'neighborhood' takes every member and the members around it in the space, fixed for the run.
  • 'state' groups the members that share a value of the state by, and every reduction over s.members reads only them.

act and capacity belong to the agent form, and check() rejects them in the symbolic form. The Galam majority rule on random groups of three, and the public goods of the groups of a lattice summed into a payoff:

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import GroupingInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import mean, where
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.models.biology.epidemiology import SpreadingInteraction
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec


class PlayerElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        s: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        payoff: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.s = s
        self.payoff = payoff


opinions = (np.random.default_rng(0).random(30) < 0.7).astype(float)
voters = GroupElement('voters', element=PlayerElement, size=30, values={'s': opinions})
galam = GroupingInteraction(
    'galam',
    target='voters',
    groups='partition',
    size=3,
    form='symbolic',
    write='s',
    function=lambda g: where(mean(g.members.s, over=g.members) > 1 / 2, 1, 0),
)
run = Simulation(System(elements=[voters], interactions=[galam]), random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=5)
print(run.trajectory_.values('voters.s').mean(axis=1).round(2).tolist())

players = LatticeElement(
    'players',
    element=PlayerElement,
    space=LatticeSpace((10, 10), neighborhood='von_neumann'),
    values={'s': (np.random.default_rng(1).random(100) < 0.5).astype(float)},
)
goods = GroupingInteraction(
    'goods',
    target='players',
    groups='neighborhood',
    form='symbolic',
    write='payoff',
    function=lambda g: 4.5 * mean(g.members.s, over=g.members) - g.member.s,
)
run = Simulation(System(elements=[players], interactions=[goods])).check().prepare().run(until=1)
print(run.trajectory_.values('players.payoff')[-1][:5].round(2).tolist())

docs.title: Coupling over the hyperedges of a member
docs.text:
The reduction hyperedges(expression, reduce='sum', size=None, weight=None) of skcomplex.core.laws.utils reduces an expression written for one hyperedge over the hyperedges around every member of a group on the nodes of a network with hyperedges, as neighbors does for one neighbour. Inside the expression s.others holds the other members of the hyperedge in its order, s.members all its members, which total, mean, count, maximum, and minimum reduce with over=s.members, and s the reading member. The reductions are those of neighbors; without a size the expression reads s.members, and only the sum, the mean, and the count run over hyperedges of several sizes. A law that reads it outside a network with hyperedges gets the issue code law-space, and a size the network lacks the code binding.

CouplingInteraction(mode='hyperedges', size=...) couples every member through it: the function reads s.member, s.others, cut to size - 1 members when the size is given, and s.members, and the default term is the sum over the other members of the difference of read. In the map form it sets the next value of write in discrete time. The three-body Kuramoto coupling over the triangles of a hypergraph, and the payoff of the public goods game summed over the hyperedges of every size around a player:

from typing import Annotated

import itertools
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import sin

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import CouplingInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import count, total
from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.compile import compile_system
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.models.biology.epidemiology import SpreadingInteraction
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec


class PlayerElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        theta: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        s: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        payoff: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.theta = theta
        self.s = s
        self.payoff = payoff


triangles = [list(nodes) for nodes in itertools.combinations(range(5), 3)]
space = NetworkSpace(nx.complete_graph(5), hyperedges=triangles)
triads = CouplingInteraction(
    'triads',
    target='oscillators',
    mode='hyperedges',
    size=3,
    read='theta',
    write='theta',
    function=lambda s: sin(s.others[0].theta + s.others[1].theta - 2 * s.member.theta),
)
oscillators = LatticeElement('oscillators', element=PlayerElement, space=space, values={'theta': np.linspace(0, 1, 5)})
problem = compile_system(System(elements=[oscillators], interactions=[triads]))
drift = problem.states.read(problem.drift(0.0, problem.initial_state, problem.initial_parameters), 'oscillators.theta')
print(np.round(drift, 3).tolist())

groups = NetworkSpace(nx.complete_graph(5), hyperedges=[[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 3, 4], [0, 4]])
players = LatticeElement('players', element=PlayerElement, space=groups, values={'s': [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0]})
goods = CouplingInteraction(
    'goods',
    target='players',
    mode='hyperedges',
    form='map',
    write='payoff',
    function=lambda s: 3 * total(s.members.s, over=s.members) / count(over=s.members) - s.member.s,
)
run = Simulation(System(elements=[players], interactions=[goods])).check().prepare().run(until=1)
print(run.trajectory_.values('players.payoff')[-1].round(2).tolist())

docs.title: Ordered phases of update laws
docs.text:
Every update law of a step reads the states at the start of the step, so a payoff and an imitation that reads it would need two steps. UpdateLaw(state, value, phase=...) names a phase, and the interactions with update laws in a phase pass theirs: GroupingInteraction in its symbolic form, ImitationInteraction in its probability form, and CouplingInteraction in its map form. The phases of the PhasesScheduleSpec of the DiscreteTime run one after the other within a step, on the NumPy and Numba backends, each reading the states the phases before it set; laws without a phase run in the default phase, first unless the schedule places it. The draws of a step are made once, before the first phase. A law in a phase the schedule does not declare raises ValidationError. The public goods game of a lattice plays in the phase play and copies a random neighbour by the Fermi rule in the phase imitate:

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import GroupingInteraction, ImitationInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import mean
from skcomplex.core.spaces import DiscreteTime, LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.specs import PhaseSpec, PhasesScheduleSpec, StateSpec


class PlayerElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        s: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        payoff: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.s = s
        self.payoff = payoff


players = LatticeElement(
    'players',
    element=PlayerElement,
    space=LatticeSpace((20, 20), neighborhood='von_neumann'),
    values={'s': (np.random.default_rng(0).random(400) < 0.5).astype(float)},
)
play = GroupingInteraction(
    'play',
    target='players',
    groups='neighborhood',
    form='symbolic',
    write='payoff',
    function=lambda g: 5.5 * mean(g.members.s, over=g.members) - g.member.s,
    phase='play',
)
imitation = ImitationInteraction(
    'imitation', target='players', state='s', rule='fermi', form='probability', intensity=2.0, phase='imitate'
)
time = DiscreteTime(schedule=PhasesScheduleSpec((PhaseSpec('play'), PhaseSpec('imitate'))))
system = System(elements=[players], interactions=[play, imitation], time=time)
run = Simulation(system, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=30)
print(round(float(run.trajectory_.values('players.s')[-1].mean()), 2) > 0.5)

docs.title: Reductions over neighbourhoods
docs.text:
neighbors(expression, over=..., reduce=..., weight=...) reduces an expression written for one neighbour, through s.other, over the neighbours of every member: the neighbours of a network by default, a layer with AdjacencyNeighborhood(layer=label), the neighbourhood of a lattice, or in a continuous space RadiusNeighborhood(r), NearestNeighborhood(k), and ConeNeighborhood(r, angle). The reductions are 'sum', 'mean', 'count', 'max', 'min', and 'normalized-mean'. A weight may read the state of the edge group of the layer through a role of an interaction, as the weight of the edge that joins the member to its neighbour. The Kuramoto coupling on a network is RateLaw(s.theta, s.omega + s.K * neighbors(sin(s.other.theta - s.theta), reduce='mean')).

from typing import Annotated

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import Interaction
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import neighbors
from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.specs import RoleSpec, StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.compile import compile_system


class NodeElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.u = u


class LinkElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, w: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.w = w


class DiffusionInteraction(Interaction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, nodes: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], links: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()]):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.nodes = nodes
        self.links = links

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.nodes.u, neighbors(s.nodes.other.u - s.nodes.u, weight=s.links.w))]


space = NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(3))
system = System(
    elements=[
        LatticeElement('nodes', element=NodeElement, space=space, values={'u': [0.0, 1.0, 4.0]}),
        GroupElement('links', element=LinkElement, space=space, on='edges', values={'w': [1.0, 10.0]}),
    ],
    interactions=[DiffusionInteraction('diffusion', nodes='nodes', links='links')],
)
problem = compile_system(system)
drift = problem.drift(0.0, problem.initial_state, problem.initial_parameters)
print(problem.states.read(drift, 'nodes.u').tolist())

Validation reports a reduction whose neighbourhood the space does not offer, such as RadiusNeighborhood(1.0) on a network, with the code law-space, and a layer the network lacks with the code binding.

docs.title: Connected components
docs.text:
components(active, over=None, reduce='label') reduces over the connected components of the active links between the members of a group. The links are the pairs of neighbours of the neighbourhood, the graph of the network by default, and the expression active, written for one link as in neighbors, reads s.other, s, and the edge group of a role, so a condition on both ends gives site percolation and an edge weight bond percolation. The reductions are 'label', the smallest member of the component of every member, 'size', the size of that component, 'largest', the size of the largest component, and 'giant', 1 for the members of the largest component. The NumPy backend runs SciPy's connected_components on the active links, and the Numba backend a union-find. The occupied sites of a path:

from typing import Annotated

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import components, where
from skcomplex.core.spaces import NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.compile import compile_system
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec


class SiteElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, occupied: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.occupied = occupied

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        both = where(s.occupied > 0, 1, 0) * where(s.other.occupied > 0, 1, 0)
        return [RateLaw(s.occupied, components(both, reduce='size'))]


sites = LatticeElement(
    'sites',
    element=SiteElement,
    space=NetworkSpace(nx.path_graph(6)),
    values={'occupied': [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]},
)
problem = compile_system(System(elements=[sites]))
drift = problem.drift(0.0, problem.initial_state, problem.initial_parameters)
print(problem.states.read(drift, 'sites.occupied').tolist())

docs.title: Topology requests
docs.text:
A variable group on the sites or edges of a network, GroupElement(..., on='sites', variable=True, capacity=n), holds rows for up to capacity members, of which the members present are marked active. The NumPy and Numba backends run such groups with fixed array shapes: laws leave the free rows unchanged, reductions read the members present, and neighbourhoods and interactions over neighbours read the edges present. A TopologyRequestSpec of the kind 'add-node', 'remove-node', 'add-edge', 'remove-edge', or 'rewire' is the target of update and jump laws: UpdateLaw(request, probability) fires the request with a probability at every step for every member or edge its law runs for, and JumpLaw(rate, {request: 1}) fires it at a rate. The iteration and Gillespie steppers apply the requests between steps. A request that joins nodes draws the new ends with weights from toward, a module-level function of the namespace of a candidate node, such as one that returns neighbors(1) for its degree. A request on a group that is not variable gets the validation issue group-fixed, and a full capacity raises CapacityError.

Trajectories hold the values of absent members as NaN, and trajectory.network(frame) returns the nodes and edges present at a frame. Rerun draws the nodes present and the edges at every frame where they change. Barabási-Albert growth adds one node with two edges at every step:

from typing import Annotated

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import UpdateLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import neighbors
from skcomplex.core.spaces import DiscreteTime, NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec, TopologyRequestSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


class NodeElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, age: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.age = age

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [UpdateLaw(s.age, s.age + 1)]


class LinkElement(Element):
    pass


def degree(node):
    return neighbors(1)


class GrowthElement(Element):
    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [UpdateLaw(TopologyRequestSpec('add-node', edges=2, toward=degree), 1)]


system = System(
    elements=[
        GroupElement('nodes', element=NodeElement, on='sites', variable=True, capacity=203),
        GroupElement('links', element=LinkElement, on='edges', variable=True, capacity=403),
        GrowthElement('growth'),
    ],
    space=NetworkSpace(nx.complete_graph(3)),
    time=DiscreteTime(),
)
trajectory = Simulation(system, dt=50.0, random_state=1).check().prepare().run(until=200).trajectory_
snapshot = trajectory.network(-1)
degrees = np.bincount(np.concatenate([snapshot.sources, snapshot.targets]))
print(snapshot.nodes.size, snapshot.sources.size, int(degrees.max()) > 10)

A network grows by hyperedges with TopologyInteraction(action='add-node', hyperedge=k), or TopologyRequestSpec('add-node', hyperedge=k): every new node forms a hyperedge of k members with k - 1 existing nodes and joins each of them by an edge. The first two are the ends of an edge drawn uniformly, the others are drawn by toward, and the new node is the last member, so an edge joins the first two members of every hyperedge. The hyperedges are the rows of a variable group on the hyperedges, GroupElement(on='hyperedges', variable=True, capacity=n), so the initial hyperedges and the new ones have one size, hyperedge interactions read the hyperedges present at every step, and trajectory.network(frame).hyperedges holds the members of those present at a frame. A network grows by triangles from one triangle:

import networkx as nx

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import TopologyInteraction
from skcomplex.core.spaces import DiscreteTime, NetworkSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation

system = System(
    elements=[
        GroupElement('nodes', element=Element, on='sites', variable=True, capacity=23),
        GroupElement('links', element=Element, on='edges', variable=True, capacity=43),
        GroupElement('triangles', element=Element, on='hyperedges', variable=True, capacity=21),
    ],
    interactions=[TopologyInteraction('growth', action='add-node', hyperedge=3)],
    space=NetworkSpace(nx.complete_graph(3), hyperedges=[[0, 1, 2]]),
    time=DiscreteTime(),
)
trajectory = Simulation(system, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=20).trajectory_
print(trajectory.network(-1).hyperedges.shape, trajectory.network(-1).sources.size)

docs.title: Kinetic models of active particles
docs.text: The kinetic theory of active particles of Bellomo et al. describes a population by the distribution of its members over an activity variable, such as wealth, an opinion, or the progression of a tumour cell. Encounters between particles change the distribution, and its moments give the macroscopic quantities.

docs.title: Distributions as site groups
docs.text:
A distribution over n activity values is a group on the sites of a lattice of n sites, one member per activity, GroupElement(label, element=E, size=n, on='sites'). The element declares one real state, the density at the member's activity, and the activity values are an array that the laws and the moments receive. No distribution component is needed, and a population of several functional subsystems is several such groups.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import oo
from sage.sets.real_set import RealSet

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec


class WealthDensityElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, f: Annotated[float, StateSpec(domain=RealSet.closed_open(0, oo))] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.f = f


classes = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 9)
profile = np.exp(-((classes - 0.5) ** 2) / 0.05)
wealth = GroupElement('wealth', element=WealthDensityElement, size=9, on='sites', values={'f': profile / profile.sum()})

docs.title: Encounters
docs.text:
EncounterLaw(candidate, field, rate, transition, test=None) declares that a candidate particle at activity h meets a field particle at activity k at the rate eta[h, k], and ends at activity i with the probability A[h, k, i]. An interaction returns it with roles bound to the candidate and field groups, and the compiler derives the gain and loss equations

df_i/dt = sum_hk eta[h, k] A[h, k, i] f_h g_k - f_i sum_k eta[i, k] g_k

without any hand derivation. The candidate moves into the test group when it is given, such as a cell that mutates into another subsystem.

  • BilinearLaw(target, first, second, rate, outcomes=None) changes the target at the signed rate r[h, k]. A positive rate creates a particle without removing the first density, at its activity or at an activity drawn from outcomes, and a negative rate with the first density as the target removes it.
  • Rates and probabilities are numbers or parameter expressions, scalars or arrays. Only the nonzero probabilities enter the lowering, as sparse contractions on NumPy and one fused loop on Numba.
  • The two laws need continuous time, a lattice space, and real states, and validation reports a law whose system lacks them, with the fix to declare them.
  • Validation reports the encounters whose probabilities do not sum to one over the outcomes, with the candidate and field activities and the sum, before compilation.
  • A system with encounters has no exact Jacobian, so implicit solvers estimate it by finite differences.

```python continuation from skcomplex.core.interactions import Interaction from skcomplex.core.laws import EncounterLaw from skcomplex.core.spaces import ContinuousTime, LatticeSpace from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, RoleSpec from skcomplex.core.system import System from skcomplex.engine.compile import PassCompiler from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation

def exchange_table(cooperation, competition): table = np.zeros((9, 9, 9)) for candidate in range(9): for field in range(9): gap = int(np.sign(field - candidate)) for outcome, probability in ((candidate + gap, cooperation), (candidate - gap, competition)): if gap and 0 <= outcome < 9: table[candidate, field, outcome] += probability table[candidate, field, candidate] += 1 - table[candidate, field].sum() return table

class ExchangeInteraction(Interaction): def init(self, label, *, population: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], eta: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0): super().init(label) self.population = population self.eta = eta

def _get_laws(self, s):
    return [EncounterLaw(s.population.f, s.population.f, s.eta, exchange_table(0.2, 0.3))]

economy = System( elements=[wealth], interactions=[ExchangeInteraction('exchange', population='wealth')], space=LatticeSpace(9, boundary='fixed'), time=ContinuousTime(), ) densities = Simulation(economy, dt=10.0).check().prepare().run(until=100).trajectory_.values('wealth.f') print(densities.sum(axis=1)[[0, -1]].round(12).tolist(), densities[-1].round(3).tolist()) print(PassCompiler().check().prepare(economy).report_.ok) 

### External actions

External actions need no primitive of their own.

- A micro-scale action, such as a welfare policy that acts on the transitions of the wealth classes, is an encounter
  whose field role binds a group with fixed states, a group no law changes.
- A macro-scale action, such as a recruitment of security forces proportional to the mean criminality, is a `RateLaw`
  that reads the moments of a distribution.

```python continuation
class PolicyInteraction(Interaction):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        population: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        government: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()],
        tax: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 0.2,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.population = population
        self.government = government
        self.tax = tax

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        rates, table = np.zeros((9, 1)), np.zeros((9, 1, 9))
        for candidate in range(9):
            outcome = candidate + 1 if candidate < 3 else candidate - 1 if candidate >= 6 else candidate
            rates[candidate, 0] = float(outcome != candidate)
            table[candidate, 0, outcome] = 1.0
        return [EncounterLaw(s.population.f, s.government.f, rates * s.tax, table)]


welfare = System(
    elements=[wealth, GroupElement('government', element=WealthDensityElement, size=1, values={'f': 1.0})],
    interactions=[
        ExchangeInteraction('exchange', population='wealth'),
        PolicyInteraction('policy', population='wealth', government='government'),
    ],
    space=LatticeSpace(9, boundary='fixed'),
    time=ContinuousTime(),
)
print(Simulation(welfare, dt=10.0).check().prepare().run(until=100).trajectory_.values('wealth.f')[-1].round(3).tolist())

docs.title: Moments
docs.text:
moment(expression, order, coordinates) is the reduction sum_j c_j^r f_j over the members of a group, with the coordinate c_j of every member, such as its activity. The order-0 moment is the density. normalized=True divides by the density, so the normalized order-1 moment is the mean activity, and central=True takes the moment about the mean, so the central order-2 moment is the variance. Moments are expressions of total with a shared row of weights, a vector with one weight per reduced member, so laws read them and observables record them. An observable of a group receives the namespace of one member, and its function must be defined at module level so that it pickles.

```python continuation from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import moment from skcomplex.specs import ObservableSpec

def mean_wealth(s): return moment(s.f, 1, classes, normalized=True)

def wealth_variance(s): return moment(s.f, 2, classes, central=True)

observables = [ ObservableSpec('mean_wealth', mean_wealth, group='wealth'), ObservableSpec('wealth_variance', wealth_variance, group='wealth'), ] trajectory = Simulation(economy, dt=10.0, observables=observables).check().prepare().run(until=100).trajectory_ variance = trajectory.values('wealth_variance') print(round(float(trajectory.values('mean_wealth')[-1]), 3), variance[[0, -1]].round(3).tolist()) 

### The particle solver

`KineticSolver(n, dt)` runs the same declarations by direct simulation Monte Carlo. It holds every density as counts
of particles of one mass, with `n` particles for the largest initial density. In every step a candidate particle
encounters with the probability `1 - exp(-lambda_h dt)`, where `lambda_h = sum_k eta[h, k] g_k`, and picks its field
activity and outcome in proportion to `eta[h, k] A[h, k, i] g_k`. A proliferation adds a Poisson number of particles
and a destruction removes a binomial number. The state holds the empirical densities, so trajectories match the ODE
form, and the error against the ODE solution falls as one over the square root of `n`. The solver supports continuous
time, lattice spaces, site groups, and encounter laws only, so validation reports a rate law with it and lists the
solvers that run it.

```python continuation
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import KineticSolver

sampled = Simulation(economy, dt=10.0, solver=KineticSolver(n=20_000), random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=100)
print(round(float(np.abs(sampled.trajectory_.values('wealth.f')[-1] - densities[-1]).sum()), 2))
print(PassCompiler(solver=KineticSolver()).check().prepare(welfare).report_.ok)

docs.title: Levels
docs.text:
CoarseGrainAnalysis(over=values) coarse-grains in state space: it bins the values of a state of a group's members, from their initial values or from a frame of a trajectory, over given values, every member counting at the nearest value, so the densities sum to 1 and start a distribution site group. Members drawn from a distribution are values sampled with NumPy in proportion to the densities, and the group's constructor builds them. A model can then run one level in a partition of a co-simulation and feed another level its moments.

```python continuation from skcomplex.analysis import CoarseGrainAnalysis

class TraderElement(Element): def init(self, label, *, w: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0): super().init(label) self.w = w

profile = densities[-1] / densities[-1].sum() wealths = classes[np.random.default_rng(0).choice(classes.size, size=1000, p=profile)] traders = GroupElement('traders', element=TraderElement, size=1000, values={'w': wealths}, variable=True) density = CoarseGrainAnalysis(over=classes).check().prepare(traders.values['w']).run().field_ binned = GroupElement('wealth', element=WealthDensityElement, size=classes.size, on='sites', values={'f': density}) print(round(float(density.sum()), 6), round(float(density @ classes), 3), round(float(traders.values['w'].mean()), 3)) 

The library has `kinetic_wealth_welfare` in `skcomplex.models.economics.econophysics`, `immune_competition` in
`skcomplex.models.biology.oncology`, `kinetic_opinion` in `skcomplex.models.social.opinion_dynamics`, and `evacuation`
and `criminality` in `skcomplex.models.social.crowds`. `evacuation` holds a crowd on a network of rooms as a site group
on a two-dimensional lattice indexed by room and speed class, whose walking encounters read the doors of the building.

### Automata on groups

A cellular automaton needs only a group: its cells are the elements, and a cell at `g` reads the cells at `g s` for
the elements `s` of a finite memory set (Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert 2023). `CayleySpace(group, ball=r)` is the
Cayley graph of a finitely generated group on the ball of radius `r` in its generators and their inverses, and
`CayleySpace(group)` without a ball is the whole of a finite group, such as a finite quotient, where configurations are
periodic. A group space is a space with sites, so `LocalRuleLaw`, `SampleLaw`, and the other lattice laws run on it
with the NumPy and Numba backends, and a run reads only its neighbour table. Preparing the space enumerates its sites,
numbered by word length: `generators_` names the generators, `words_` gives the shortest word of every site,
`ball_sizes_` gives the growth of the balls, and cells outside a ball read the space's `fill`. The memory set is a
`MemoryNeighborhood` of words such as `'a'`, `'a^-1'`, or `'a*b'`, with `'1'` for the cell itself, and
`GeneratorNeighborhood(generators)` gives the identity followed by every generator and its inverse.

The group is a native Sage or GAP group, so a group given by any presentation whose word problem a library solves
works:

- A free group, `libgap.FreeGroup(['a', 'b'])`, reduces its words directly, and a finitely presented group,
  `free / relators`, is solved by Knuth-Bendix completion with KBMAG in GAP. A presentation it cannot complete raises
  `SpaceError`, which asks for a finite quotient.
- An automaton group of the AutomGrp package, such as `libgap.AutomatonGroup('t = (1, t)(1, 2)')` for the adding
  machine, has its elements told apart by their action on a level of the tree, and `libgap.PermGroupOnLevel(group, n)`
  is its finite quotient on level `n`.
- A Sage `PermutationGroup` or `MatrixGroup` compares its elements directly.

GAP comes with the `passagemath-gap` dependency and starts on the first ball that needs it. A ball whose size bound
exceeds `max_sites`, 100,000 by default, raises `SpaceTooLargeError` before GAP is called, and the compiler reports it as
`space-too-large` with the largest radius that fits. A group space lacks the regular geometry of a square lattice and
an image layout, so validation reports a checkerboard schedule as `schedule-unsupported` and an image visual as
`visual-unsupported`. Groups on group spaces stream to Rerun with `CayleyVisual`: nodes on rings by word length,
colored by state, with the edges of the generators logged once.

```python
from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_gap import PermutationGroup, libgap
from sage.sets.finite_enumerated_set import FiniteEnumeratedSet

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, LatticeElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import LocalRuleLaw
from skcomplex.specs import TotalisticSpec
from skcomplex.core.spaces import CayleySpace, GeneratorNeighborhood
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation

tree = CayleySpace(libgap.FreeGroup(['a', 'b']), ball=4).check().prepare()
memory = GeneratorNeighborhood(tree.generators_)


class MajorityElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, alive: Annotated[float, StateSpec(domain=FiniteEnumeratedSet([0, 1]))] = 0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.alive = alive

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [LocalRuleLaw(s.alive, memory, TotalisticSpec({3: 1, 4: 1, 5: 1}))]


cells = (np.random.default_rng(0).random(tree.size_) < 0.5).astype(float)
majority = System(elements=[LatticeElement('cells', element=MajorityElement, space=tree, values={'alive': cells})])
print(tree.ball_sizes_, Simulation(majority, dt=1).check().prepare().run(until=3).trajectory_.values('cells.alive').shape)
print(CayleySpace(PermutationGroup([[(1, 2)], [(1, 2, 3)]])).check().prepare().words_)

Named groups are realizations of the automata models: free_group, heisenberg, lamplighter, baumslag_solitar, and grigorchuk_group of skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata. The Grigorchuk group, which acts on the binary tree by a = (1, 1)(0 1), b = (a, c), c = (a, d), d = (1, b), is not finitely presented, and its balls grow faster than any polynomial and slower than any exponential. Its action on level 3 of the tree is a finite quotient.

from sage.all__sagemath_gap import libgap

from skcomplex.core.spaces import CayleySpace
from skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata import grigorchuk_group

ball = CayleySpace(grigorchuk_group(), ball=6).check().prepare()
quotient = CayleySpace(libgap.PermGroupOnLevel(grigorchuk_group(), 3)).check().prepare()
print(ball.ball_sizes_, quotient.size_)

Theory of automata. skcomplex.analysis decides the properties the theory studies on finite universes, where they are decidable: periodic configurations on a torus or a finite quotient, and patterns on windows. The checks do not decide them on infinite groups. Automaton(space, neighborhood, rule, states) of skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata is the map on configurations of a local rule, with step and run, and AutomatonAnalysis prepares on it.

  • The kinds 'injective' and 'surjective', which agree on a finite universe, enumerate the configurations of small universes and solve a SAT encoding with PySAT on larger ones. 'pre-injective' asks whether two configurations that differ only inside a window can share their image.
  • 'garden-of-eden' finds a pattern without a preimage, by enumeration or by SAT on random patterns.
  • 'inverse' finds the rule of the inverse of a reversible automaton with the smallest memory up to max_radius, and 'compose' gives the automaton of its composition with a second one.
from skcomplex.specs import OuterTotalisticSpec, TableSpec
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeNeighborhood, LatticeSpace, MooreNeighborhood

from skcomplex.analysis import AutomatonAnalysis
from skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata import Automaton

life = Automaton(LatticeSpace((6, 6)), MooreNeighborhood(), OuterTotalisticSpec({(0, 3): 1, (1, 2): 1, (1, 3): 1}))
print(AutomatonAnalysis('surjective').check().prepare(life).run().surjective_)
print(AutomatonAnalysis('garden-of-eden', random_state=0).check().prepare(life).run().pattern_ is not None)
shift = Automaton(LatticeSpace(8), LatticeNeighborhood(((1,),)), TableSpec({(1,): 1}))
back = AutomatonAnalysis('inverse').check().prepare(shift).run().inverse_
composition = AutomatonAnalysis('compose', second=back).check().prepare(shift).run().composition_
print(composition.step([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1]).tolist())

Linear automata and subshifts. LinearAutomaton(space, neighborhood, coefficients, field) is the element sum_s a_s s of the group ring over 'GF(p)' or 'QQ'. On a finite universe it is a matrix whose rank decides injectivity, surjectivity, and pre-injectivity together, and on Z^d, with infinite=True, its Laurent polynomial decides them: it is invertible when the polynomial is a monomial and surjective when it is not zero. Subshift(neighborhood, forbidden) holds the configurations without forbidden patterns: it checks configurations, counts the admissible ones of a window, and samples them by a Markov chain of single-cell moves. Both are models of skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata, and AutomatonAnalysis tells the three models apart by their methods. AutomatonAnalysis('entropy', windows=windows) gives log |X_F| / |F| along windows F, and AutomatonAnalysis('difference') the cells where two runs differ after one cell changes. EntropyAnalysis('rate') of the frames of a run as columns gives the spatial entropy rate of every frame, which never increases under an automaton.

from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeNeighborhood, LatticeSpace

from skcomplex.analysis import AutomatonAnalysis
from skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata import LinearAutomaton, Subshift

laplacian = LinearAutomaton(LatticeSpace(5), LatticeNeighborhood(((-1,), (0,), (1,))), (1, -2, 1), 'GF(2)')
golden = Subshift(LatticeNeighborhood(((0,), (1,))), [(1, 1)])
print(AutomatonAnalysis('injective').check().prepare(laplacian).run().injective_)
print(AutomatonAnalysis('surjective', infinite=True).check().prepare(laplacian).run().surjective_)
print([golden.count(LatticeSpace(length, boundary='fixed')) for length in range(1, 8)])
windows = [LatticeSpace(24, boundary='fixed')]
print(AutomatonAnalysis('entropy', windows=windows).check().prepare(golden).run().entropy_.round(3))

The library has free_group_automaton, lamplighter_automaton, heisenberg_automaton, baumslag_solitar_automaton, grigorchuk_automaton, the Laplacian linear_ring_automaton, and the golden mean shift subshifts in skcomplex.models.computer_science.automata.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
A field holds one value per site of a lattice or per node of a network. FieldElement(label, element=..., space=..., boundary=..., values=...) places a member of an element type on every site, and the laws of the type, written for one site, read the neighbouring sites through differential operators. The method of lines turns a field into ordinary differential equations, so every ODE solver and backend runs it.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import laplacian
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


class HeatElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        D: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.u = u
        self.D = D

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.u, s.D * laplacian(s.u))]


initial = np.zeros(400)
initial[200] = 20.0
space = LatticeSpace(400, spacing=0.05)
rod = FieldElement('rod', element=HeatElement, space=space, boundary={'u': 'zero-flux'}, values={'u': initial})
trajectory = Simulation(System(elements=[rod]), dt=0.1).check().prepare().run(until=0.5).trajectory_
heat = trajectory.values('rod.u')
print(round(float(heat[-1].max()), 3), heat.sum(axis=1)[[0, -1]].round(6).tolist())
  • laplacian(u) lowers to the 2d + 1-point stencil divided by the squared spacing, and to the graph Laplacian on a NetworkSpace. gradient(u, n_dim) and divergence(vector) use central differences, and advection(u, velocity) upwind differences. Operators apply to any expression of the field's states and parameters, and nest.
  • boundary={'u': 'periodic' | 'zero-flux' | ('fixed', value)} sets each state's edges. Zero flux mirrors the field and conserves its total, and fixed edges read the given value. A lattice's own boundary is the default.
  • The equations keep the operators, diff(u(t), t) == D*laplacian(u(t)), while the backends evaluate the stencils, fused into one compiled loop on Numba for lattices.
  • problem.stable_step is the diffusive limit h^2 / (2 d D) of explicit steps, and fixed-step solvers whose dt exceeds it warn before the run with the limit.

Agents on a grid of the same shape couple to a field in co-simulation. A rule reads the field at a cell with model.field('ground/pheromone.level', cell) and adds to it with model.deposit(name, cell, amount), and the deposits reach the field at the next synchronisation point. Lattice fields stream to Rerun as images. The library has heat_diffusion, fisher_kpp, gray_scott, brusselator, fitzhugh_nagumo, schnakenberg, and pheromone_foraging, such as gray_scott in skcomplex.models.chemistry.pattern_formation and heat_diffusion in skcomplex.models.physics.heat.

docs.title: Discretizations and stiff solvers
docs.text:
The same laws of a field run with another discretization by changing FieldElement(..., discretization=...).

  • 'spectral' fields on periodic lattices multiply Fourier modes, with the two-thirds rule removing aliasing from every operator, so laplacian(u) is exact for smooth fields. inverse_laplacian(u) solves Poisson equations, and symmetry={'u': (None, 'odd')} keeps a state odd or even along an axis, which represents walls on a doubled lattice. LatticeSpace(spacing=(dx, dy)) sets a spacing per axis.
  • 'finite-volume' fields take FluxLaw(state, flux)s, du/dt + divergence(flux) = 0, updated with MUSCL reconstruction, minmod or van Leer limiters, and Rusanov or exact Godunov fluxes. SSPRKSolver steps them by the CFL condition and by the stability limit of their Laplacian rates at the current parameters, and conserves their totals.
  • 'finite-element' fields live on a MeshSpace of the points and cells of a scikit-fem mesh, such as MeshSpace(grid.p, grid.t) for grid = skfem.MeshTri.init_lshaped().refined(3), with stiffness and mass matrices from scikit-fem and boundary values that can be functions of the coordinates. They stream to Rerun as colored meshes.

The compiler splits the rate of every field into a linear part with constant coefficients, such as D * laplacian(u) or -laplacian(laplacian(u)), and a nonlinear remainder. IMEXEulerSolver, IMEX2Solver, and CrankNicolsonSolver treat the linear part implicitly, with sparse solves for finite differences and finite elements and solves per Fourier mode for spectral fields. ETDRK4Solver integrates it exactly per mode, coupled states included, so stiff equations take steps far beyond the explicit limit.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import divergence, laplacian
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import ETDRK4Solver


class ChaosElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.u = u

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.u, -divergence([s.u**2 / 2]) - laplacian(s.u) - laplacian(laplacian(s.u)))]


positions = np.arange(1, 129) * 32 * np.pi / 128
line = FieldElement(
    'line',
    element=ChaosElement,
    space=LatticeSpace(128, spacing=32 * np.pi / 128),
    values={'u': np.cos(positions / 16) * (1 + np.sin(positions / 16))},
    discretization='spectral',
)
state = Simulation(System(elements=[line]), dt=10, solver=ETDRK4Solver(dt=0.25)).check().prepare().run(until=100).state_
print(round(float(np.abs(state).max()), 1))

The implicit methods of ScipyODESolver are the stiff path for finite-difference and finite element fields, with adaptive error control that the fixed-step split steppers lack. The compiler derives the sparsity pattern of the Jacobian from the laws: member and shared reads, the neighbour tables of stencils, the sparse matrices of finite elements, the reconstruction stencils of finite volumes, and dense blocks where couplings are known only at run time, such as pairs, spectral operators, and callables. ScipyODESolver(method='BDF') and ScipyODESolver(method='Radau') receive the pattern, so SciPy estimates the Jacobian with one drift evaluation per group of independent columns and factors it with sparse LU, and LSODA receives the half bandwidths of a pattern narrower than a tenth of the size. The option jacobian selects the path: 'auto' by default, 'exact' for the sparse Jacobian of the laws differentiated by Sage, which laws without a symbolic form cannot give, and 'dense' for the dense estimate. Explicit methods ignore it, and RK45 warns when one call spans more than 1000 stable steps of the diffusion of a field.

from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation

from skcomplex.engine.solvers import ScipyODESolver
from skcomplex.models.biology.ecology import fisher_kpp

stiff = fisher_kpp(400, D=1.0, spacing=0.05)
simulation = Simulation(stiff, dt=1.0, solver=ScipyODESolver(method='BDF')).check().prepare().run(until=5)
print(simulation.stepper_.jacobian_pattern_.nnz, simulation.state_.max().round(3))

On Fisher-KPP on 4000 points, whose largest eigenvalue is about 1600, run to t = 10, BDF with the dense estimate took 35 to 50 s, against about 0.2 s with the pattern, 0.3 s with the exact Jacobian, 0.7 s for Radau with the pattern, and 0.8 s for CrankNicolsonSolver(dt=0.01). Spectral fields keep ETDRK4Solver and the IMEX steppers, which win there because their linear part is diagonal in Fourier space while its pattern is dense.

skcomplex.models.physics.fluids.incompressible_flow(shape, size, nu=..., forcing=..., buoyancy=...) builds two-dimensional incompressible flow in vorticity-streamfunction form, with Boussinesq convection when buoyancy gives Ra and Pr. The library has kuramoto_sivashinsky, complex_ginzburg_landau, swift_hohenberg, and heat_l_shape in the subfields fluids, pattern_formation, and heat of skcomplex.models.physics, and burgers, shallow_water, decaying_turbulence, and rayleigh_benard in skcomplex.models.physics.fluids.

docs.title: Nonlocal operators
docs.text:
Three operators of skcomplex.core.laws.utils read beyond the nearest sites, and a law writes them as a reference writes them:

  • inverse_helmholtz(expression, screening, boundary=None) is the solution of (laplacian - screening**2) psi = expression, and inverse_laplacian(u) is its case without screening. It runs on spectral fields, on finite-difference lattices with periodic, zero-flux, or fixed edges, where the fast transforms of SciPy invert the stencil that laplacian uses, and on networks and meshes with a sparse factorization. An operand that mixes states of different boundaries needs boundary=.
  • convolve(expression, kernel, radius=None) sums an expression over the sites of a lattice against a kernel written in the symbols displacement(axis) and the parameters. The kernel is sampled when the problem is compiled, wraps around periodic edges, and is cut at fixed and zero-flux edges, where the operand is padded with the fixed value or its mirror image.
  • shifted(expression, offset, order=1) reads an expression at a physical displacement, one component per axis, which may depend on the states. A displacement of whole sites reads the neighbour tables and stays compilable to Numba, and any other one interpolates with order=1 or order=3, following the boundary of the field.

The stencil operators read a nonlocal result at the neighbouring sites, so partial and gradient apply to an inverted streamfunction. Laws with these operators run on the NumPy backend, except whole-site reads. The sparsity pattern of the Jacobian marks a convolution as coupling the sites within its radius and an inversion as dense, so implicit solvers stay correct but slow, and explicit or exponential solvers suit them best. An observable may use them too, which streams a streamfunction as an image.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np
from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import exp, pi, sqrt

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import RateInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import convolve, displacement, inverse_helmholtz, partial, shifted
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec


class SiteElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        *,
        u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0,
        k: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 2.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.u = u
        self.k = k


def rate_of(rate):
    centers = np.arange(128) * 0.1
    values = {'u': np.exp(-((centers - 6.4) ** 2))}
    line = FieldElement('line', element=SiteElement, space=LatticeSpace(128, spacing=0.1), values=values)
    interaction = RateInteraction('rate', target='line', state='u', rate=rate)
    simulation = Simulation(System(elements=[line], interactions=[interaction]), dt=0.05)
    return simulation.check().prepare().run(until=0.2).trajectory_.values('line.u')


def smoothing(s):
    kernel = exp(-displacement(0) ** 2) / sqrt(pi)
    return convolve(s.target.u, kernel) - s.target.u


def screened_drift(s):
    return partial(inverse_helmholtz(s.target.u, s.target.k), 0)


def look_ahead(s):
    return shifted(s.target.u, [0.25 + s.target.u]) - s.target.u


for rate in (smoothing, screened_drift, look_ahead):
    print(rate.__name__, rate_of(rate)[-1].sum().round(3))

The misuses are issues of the compiler's report, each with the path of the law and a fix: law-space for a convolution or a shifted read on a network or a mesh and for a spectral operator on a lattice without periodic edges, kernel-state for a kernel that reads a state, screening for a screening that reads a state or whose square can be negative, and operator-spaces for an operand that reads fields of more than one space.

A CouplingInteraction on a field sums a function of both ends over the neighbours of every site, reading a fixed boundary value as laplacian does. A constant times s.other.u - s.member.u lowers to laplacian, so spectral and finite-element fields keep their own operator.

from typing import Annotated

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import CouplingInteraction
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.models.biology.epidemiology import SpreadingInteraction
from skcomplex.specs import StateSpec


class CellElement(Element):
    def __init__(self, label, *, u: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 0.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.u = u


cells = FieldElement('cells', element=CellElement, space=LatticeSpace(32), values={'u': np.eye(32)[16]})
exchange = CouplingInteraction(
    'exchange',
    target='cells',
    read='u',
    write='u',
    function=lambda s: 0.2 * (s.other.u - s.member.u),
)
system = System(elements=[cells], interactions=[exchange])
trajectory = Simulation(system, dt=0.5).check().prepare().run(until=2.0).trajectory_
print(trajectory.values('cells.u')[-1].sum().round(6))

amari_neural_field holds a bump with a convolution, double_gyre streams the streamfunction of a closed basin, gkt_traffic brakes on the traffic read ahead, and active_viscoelastic_gel solves its force balance at every step.

docs.title: Phase-space fields
docs.text:
A kinetic equation evolves a density over position and over classes such as velocity or orientation. Particles stream through position at their velocity, forces push them through velocity, and collisions redistribute them over velocity at a fixed position. A phase space is a lattice whose axes are the product of these, so FieldElement holds one value per point, and its laws are written for one point.

No library fits: py-pde stops at three dimensions and has no class axes, pylbm and lbmpy hold a few discrete velocities, Dedalus is GPL with no wheels, Struphy is specific to plasmas, and no maintained Python library holds the fast spectral collision operator. So the numerics wrap scipy.fft and scipy.ndimage, and the core holds the adapters and the assembly of the collision weights.

docs.title: Phase spaces and coordinates
docs.text:
PhaseSpace(position, axes, limit=2**26) takes a position LatticeSpace and the class axes, each an AxisSpec(name, size, low, high, periodic=False) with its own cells. An interval has no flux through its ends, and a periodic axis such as an angle joins them. The position axes come first, and they keep the boundary of the lattice. The compile report holds a space-size issue for a space above its limit, with the size it would take.

coordinate(name) is the coordinate of the point a law updates along a named axis. Streaming is the drift [coordinate('v'), 0] and acceleration by a force F is the drift [0, F]. The compile report holds a law-space issue for a coordinate in a law whose group is not on a phase space with that axis.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import DensityElement, FieldElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import AdvectionInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import coordinate
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace, PhaseSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import RK4Solver
from skcomplex.specs import AxisSpec

space = PhaseSpace(LatticeSpace((32,), spacing=2 * np.pi / 32), [AxisSpec('v', 64, -6.0, 6.0)]).check().prepare()
x, v = np.arange(32) * 2 * np.pi / 32, space.coordinates_['v']
start = np.outer(1.0 + 0.5 * np.sin(x), np.exp(-(v**2) / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))
gas = FieldElement('gas', element=DensityElement, space=space, values={'f': start}, discretization='finite-volume')
stream = AdvectionInteraction('stream', target='gas', state='f', drift=lambda s: [coordinate('v'), 0])
system = System(elements=[gas], interactions=[stream])
simulation = Simulation(system, dt=0.1, solver=RK4Solver(dt=0.01)).check().prepare()
final = simulation.run(until=0.5).trajectory_.values('gas.f')[-1]
assert abs(final.sum() / start.sum() - 1.0) < 1e-12

Finite-volume, finite-difference with riemann=None, and spectral fields with riemann=None all stream on a phase space. Spectral derivatives need the axis to be periodic.

docs.title: Moments and mean fields
docs.text:
moment(expression, order, axes=names) reduces over class axes at every position, with the cell widths as weights. It is a field over position that laws read broadcast along the reduced axes, so normalized=True and central=True give the mean velocity and the temperature at every position. reduce_axes(expression, names) is the integral behind it, for the moments of cos and sin of an orientation. A drift can read a moment of its own field, and the operators of a field over position act along the position axes:

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import coordinate, gradient, inverse_laplacian, moment


def poisson_drift(s):
    return [coordinate('v'), -gradient(inverse_laplacian(1 - moment(s.target.f, 0, axes=('v',))), 1)[0]]

A drift reads another field over the position lattice through the sources of AdvectionInteraction and ConservationInteraction, broadcast along the class axes, and a RateInteraction over the position lattice reads a moment of a field on a phase space through its sources.

docs.title: Encounters and equilibria
docs.text:
EncounterInteraction on a phase space pairs classes at the same position. Without field it is a linear redistribution: a candidate at class h moves to class i at the rate eta[h] with the probability kernel[h, i]. A rate that is one expression may read the coordinate of the class of the candidate.

maximum_entropy(expression, axes, order=2) is the density exp(a + b c + d |c|^2) whose discrete moments equal those of the expression at every position, found by Newton steps, so a relaxation towards it conserves the moments to round-off:

from skcomplex.core.interactions import RelaxationInteraction
from skcomplex.core.laws.utils import maximum_entropy

relax = RelaxationInteraction('r', target='gas', state='f', goal=lambda s: maximum_entropy(s.target.f, axes=('v',)))
assert relax.check().state == 'f'

docs.title: Collisions
docs.text: EncounterInteraction(label, candidate=..., state='f', cross_section=..., factor=None) is the binary collision integral over two interval class axes. The cross-section is a function of arrays of the relative speed and the cosine of the deflection angle, and it enters the fast spectral method of Mouhot and Pareschi through a singular value decomposition, a single term for Maxwell molecules. The method uses FFT products on a grid padded by (3 + sqrt(2)) / 2, conserves the density exactly, and conserves the momentum and the energy within its spectral accuracy. factor scales the collision frequency, such as a function of the density moment for the local Enskog equation. The compile report holds a law-space issue for a collision without two interval class axes.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
• SemiLagrangianSolver(dt) advances fields whose fluxes are linear drifts a u, with a free of the state and constant along its own axis, by shifting each slice along its characteristic in the splitting of Cheng and Knorr. It is stable at any Courant number and conserves the total on periodic axes. Other fluxes raise a named error.
  • StrangSplittingSolver(transport, collision, dt) composes a half transport step, a full collision step, and a half transport step. The problem keeps the source rates, problem.sources, apart from the flux differences.
  • RK4Solver, ScipyODESolver, and the other method-of-lines solvers accept phase-space fields as well.
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import RK4Solver, SemiLagrangianSolver, StrangSplittingSolver

solver = StrangSplittingSolver(SemiLagrangianSolver(dt=0.1), RK4Solver(dt=0.01), dt=0.1)
assert solver.check().dt == 0.1

docs.title: Visualizing
docs.text: ImageVisual(slices=..., moments=...) logs the plane that fixes every axis but two, such as slices={'vy': 2}, and the moments over the class axes, as a bar series over a one-dimensional position lattice and as an image over a two-dimensional one. boltzmann_equation, bgk_equation, vlasov_equation, and enskog in physics/fluids, and bertin_droz_gregoire in physics/active_matter, are the kinetic equations of the library.

docs.title: Backends and speed
docs.text:
Compiling a system produces numeric functions with a backend. NumpyBackend evaluates every law with NumPy arrays, and NumbaBackend generates one compiled function per form, with compiled cell lists for pair interactions and compiled loops for RK4Solver, EulerMaruyamaSolver, GillespieSolver, and IterationSolver. Without a backend, Simulation picks Numba when the groups of a system hold at least 1000 members in total, because compiling takes a second or two that small systems do not win back, and problem_.backend names the backend it used.

from skcomplex.engine.backends import NumbaBackend
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import RK4Solver
from skcomplex.models.physics.statistical_mechanics import ideal_gas

simulation = Simulation(ideal_gas(50_000, random_state=0), solver=RK4Solver(dt=0.01), backend=NumbaBackend(), dt=0.01).check().prepare()
print(simulation.run(until=0.5).problem_.backend)

JaxBackend writes discrete maps and ordinary differential equations as pure JAX functions, which JAX traces, compiles, and differentiates. It is the backend of the inner model of a system that trains, and a forward backend that agrees with NumPy within 1e-10 in double precision.

Compiled kernels are cached on disk, under ~/.cache/skcomplex or the cache_dir of NumbaBackend(cache_dir=...), so running the same system again skips compilation.

A law value can be a function called once per member with CallSpec(function, arguments) of skcomplex.core.laws.utils. A Numba-compiled function runs inside the compiled kernels, and the NumPy backend calls it from Python.

from typing import Annotated

import numba

from skcomplex.core.elements import GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.interactions import Interaction
from skcomplex.core.laws import RateLaw
from skcomplex.specs import CallSpec
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, RoleSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.models.biology.common.populations import PopulationElement


@numba.njit
def saturating(t, n, r):
    return r * n / (1 + n)


class SaturationInteraction(Interaction):
    def __init__(self, label, *, target: Annotated[str, RoleSpec()], r: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec()] = 1.0):
        super().__init__(label)
        self.target = target
        self.r = r

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RateLaw(s.target.n, CallSpec(saturating, (s.target.n, s.r)))]


herds = System(
    elements=[GroupElement('herds', element=PopulationElement, size=2000, values={'n': 1.0})],
    interactions=[SaturationInteraction('growth', target='herds')],
)
print(round(float(Simulation(herds, dt=0.1).check().prepare().run(until=1).trajectory_.values('herds.n')[-1, 0]), 4))

A plain Python callable of the values, as in RateLaw(s.target.n, lambda t, values: ...), also works with the Numba backend, but runs in Python and turns off the compiled stepper loops for that kind of law.

docs.title: External backends
docs.text:
An external backend runs a whole system in a third-party solver library, and the simulation keeps its frames, trajectories, live parameters, and Rerun visualization. LammpsSolver runs particle systems in LAMMPS, which integrates them with velocity Verlet. Its pairs map pair potential classes to native LAMMPS pair styles and its fixes map interaction classes to native fixes, and the particle realizations of physics give both as LAMMPS_PAIRS and LAMMPS_FIXES.

import numpy as np

from skcomplex.core.elements import GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.spaces import ContinuousSpace
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation
from skcomplex.engine.solvers import LammpsSolver
from skcomplex.models.physics.common.particles import (
    LAMMPS_FIXES,
    LAMMPS_PAIRS,
    LangevinThermostatInteraction,
    LennardJonesInteraction,
    MassPointElement,
)

side = np.arange(10) * 1.2
grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(side, side), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2)
atoms = System(
    elements=[GroupElement('atoms', element=MassPointElement, size=100, values={'x': grid})],
    interactions=[
        LennardJonesInteraction('lj', first='atoms', second='atoms', cutoff=2.5, divisor='m'),
        LangevinThermostatInteraction('bath', target='atoms', temperature=0.5, gamma=1.0),
    ],
    space=ContinuousSpace(n_dim=2),
)
solver = LammpsSolver(dt=0.005, pairs=LAMMPS_PAIRS, fixes=LAMMPS_FIXES)
trajectory = Simulation(atoms, solver=solver, dt=0.05, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=1).trajectory_
print(trajectory.values('atoms.x').shape)

Before the first frame the backend checks the system and raises one error that lists every element, interaction, and law it cannot run. The translation is the following.

Framework LAMMPS elements and groups with a vector position of order 2, such as PointElement one atom type per element or group, whose velocities are the first derivatives of the positions and whose mass is the parameter the divisor of their interactions names, 1 without one two or three dimensions dimension 2 with fix enforce2d, or dimension 3 ContinuousSpace(extent, boundary='reflecting') fix wall/reflect at 0 and the extent ContinuousSpace(extent, boundary='periodic') periodic boundaries of the extent, shared by every group a class in pairs, such as LennardJonesInteraction its native pair style, such as pair_style lj/cut other PairCouplingInteraction with a potential pair_style lepton with the potential printed as a Lepton expression a class in fixes its native fix, such as fix addforce, fix viscous, or fix langevin any other interaction that only changes the derivatives of the positions fix external, evaluated by the framework every step

LangevinThermostatInteraction becomes fix langevin, seeded from the simulation's random state.

docs.title: Agent-based models
docs.text:
Agents are ordinary elements whose laws are rules written as code. An Element declares the states every agent holds and the parameters its group shares as annotated arguments of its __init__, and returns from _get_laws RuleLaws whose functions take the agent and the model. An element or a group whose laws include rules is an agent, and so is every member of a variable group. In a system with rules, a group whose element type has no laws is a group of passive agents that rules read and change, unless an interaction whose laws are not rules binds it. A system with rules is agent-based, runs in discrete time, and runs on MesaSolver, one Mesa step per unit of time, with every agent activated in random order. MesaSolver declares what it runs like any solver, so PassCompiler(solver=MesaSolver()).check().prepare(system).report_ holds the laws, spaces, and times it does not support.

from typing import Annotated

from sage.all__sagemath_symbolics import oo
from sage.sets.real_set import RealSet

from skcomplex.core.elements import Element, GroupElement
from skcomplex.core.laws import RuleLaw
from skcomplex.core.spaces import LatticeSpace
from skcomplex.specs import ParameterSpec, StateSpec, VisualSpec
from skcomplex.core.system import System
from skcomplex.engine.runtime import Simulation


class ForagerElement(Element):
    def __init__(
        self,
        label,
        visual=VisualSpec('agents', {'color_by': 'food'}),
        *,
        food: Annotated[float, StateSpec()] = 5.0,
        hunger: Annotated[float, ParameterSpec(domain=RealSet.closed_open(0, oo))] = 1.0,
    ):
        super().__init__(label, visual=visual)
        self.food = food
        self.hunger = hunger

    def _get_laws(self, s):
        return [RuleLaw(self.forage)]

    def forage(self, agent, model):
        cells = agent.neighbor_cells()
        agent.move_to(cells[int(model.rng.integers(len(cells)))])
        agent.food += model.rng.poisson(0.8) - agent.hunger
        if agent.food <= 0:
            agent.remove()
        elif agent.food > 10:
            agent.food /= 2
            agent.create(food=agent.food)


foragers = System(
    elements=[GroupElement('foragers', element=ForagerElement, size=50, variable=True)],
    space=LatticeSpace((30, 30), boundary='periodic'),
)
trajectory = Simulation(foragers, random_state=0).check().prepare().run(until=20).trajectory_
print(int(trajectory.values('foragers.count')[-1]), len(trajectory.agents('foragers', 20).ids))
